[[File:Sultan Barquq's Qur'an decagram.jpg|thumb|Decagrams are common in [[Islamic geometric patterns]], here in a Quran from the 14th century.]]

In [[geometry]], a '''decagram''' is a 10-point [[star polygon]]. There is one regular decagram, containing the vertices of a [[regular decagon]], but connected by every third point. Its [[Schläfli symbol]] is {{math|{{mset|10/3}}}}.<ref>{{citation|title=Gems of Geometry|first=John|last=Barnes|publisher=Springer|year=2012|isbn=9783642309649|pages=28–29|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7YCUBUd-4BQC&pg=PA28}}.</ref>

The name ''decagram'' combines a [[numeral prefix]], ''[[wikt:deca-|deca-]]'', with the [[Greek language|Greek]] suffix ''[[wikt:-gram|-gram]]'' ({{ety|el|''γραμμῆς'' (grammēs)|line}}).<ref>[https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus%3Atext%3A1999.04.0057%3Aentry%3Dgrammh%2F γραμμή], Henry George Liddell, Robert Scott, ''A Greek-English Lexicon'', on Perseus</ref>

== Applications ==
Decagrams have been used as one of the decorative motifs in [[girih tiles]].<ref>{{citation|contribution=Polyhedral Modularity in a Special Class of Decagram Based Interlocking Star Polygons|title=Bridges 2012: Mathematics, Music, Art, Architecture, Culture|first=Reza|last=Sarhangi|year=2012|url=http://archive.bridgesmathart.org/2012/bridges2012-165.pdf|pages=165–174}}.</ref>
: [[File:Girih tiles.svg|160px]]

== Isotoxal variations==
An [[isotoxal polygon]] has two vertices and one edge. There are isotoxal decagram forms, which alternates vertices at two radii. Each form has a freedom of one angle. The first is a variation of a double-wound of a pentagon {{math|{{mset|5}}}}, and last is a variation of a double-wound of a pentagram {{math|{{mset|5/2}}}}. The middle is a variation of a regular decagram, {{math|{{mset|10/3}}}}.

==Related figures==
A regular decagram is a 10-sided [[polygram (geometry)|polygram]], represented by symbol {{math|{{mset|10/''n''}}}}, containing the same vertices as regular [[decagon]]. Only one of these polygrams, {{math|{{mset|10/3}}}} (connecting every third point), forms a regular [[star polygon]], but there are also three ten-vertex polygrams which can be interpreted as regular compounds:
*{{math|{{mset|10/5}}}} is a compound of five degenerate [[digon]]s {{math|5{{mset|2}}}}
*{{math|{{mset|10/4}}}} is a compound of two [[pentagram]]s {{math|2{{mset|5/2}}}}
*{{math|{{mset|10/2}}}} is a compound of two [[pentagon]]s {{math|2{{mset|5}}}}.<ref>Regular polytopes, p 93-95, regular star polygons, regular star compounds</ref><ref>Coxeter, Introduction to Geometry, second edition, 2.8 ''Star polygons'' p.36-38</ref>

{{math|{{mset|10/2}}}} can be seen as the 2D equivalent of the 3D [[compound of dodecahedron and icosahedron]] and 4D [[compound of 120-cell and 600-cell]]; that is, the compound of two [[pentagonal polytope]]s in their respective dual positions.

{{math|{{mset|10/4}}}} can be seen as the two-dimensional equivalent of the three-dimensional [[compound of small stellated dodecahedron and great dodecahedron]] or [[compound of great icosahedron and great stellated dodecahedron]] through similar reasons. It has six four-dimensional analogues, with two of these being compounds of two self-dual star polytopes, like the pentagram itself; the [[compound of two great 120-cells]] and the [[compound of two grand stellated 120-cells]]. A full list can be seen at [[Polytope compound#Compounds with duals]].

Deeper truncations of the regular pentagon and pentagram can produce intermediate star polygon forms with ten equally spaced vertices and two edge lengths that remain [[vertex-transitive]] (any two vertices can be transformed into each other by a symmetry of the figure).<ref>The Lighter Side of Mathematics: Proceedings of the Eugène Strens Memorial Conference on Recreational Mathematics and its History, (1994), ''Metamorphoses of polygons'', [[Branko Grünbaum]].</ref><ref>*{{Cite journal | last1=Coxeter | first1=Harold Scott MacDonald | author1-link=Harold Scott MacDonald Coxeter | last2=Longuet-Higgins | first2=M. S. | last3=Miller | first3=J. C. P. | title=Uniform polyhedra | jstor=91532 | mr=0062446  | year=1954 | journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series A. Mathematical and Physical Sciences | issn=0080-4614 | volume=246 |issue=916 | pages=411 | publisher=[[The Royal Society]] | doi=10.1098/rsta.1954.0003 | bibcode=1954RSPTA.246..401C | s2cid=202575183 }}</ref><ref>Coxeter, The Densities of the Regular polytopes I, p.43 If d is odd, the truncation of the polygon {p/q} is naturally {2n/d}. But if not, it consists of two coincident {n/(d/2)}'s; two, because each side arises from an original side and once from an original vertex. Thus the density of a polygon is unaltered by truncation.</ref>
